newsitem.title: USA: Conn. utilities extend summer power plan to winter.
newsitem.headline: Conn. utilities extend summer power plan to winter.

text.p: Connecticut's electric utilities plan this winter to extend emergency power measures implemented during summer amid ongoing outages at all four nuclear power stations in the state.
"Most of the contingency plan from the summer we'll continue," said United Illuminating Co spokeswoman Fran Mayko. "All actions will continue for the time being."

Connecticut utilities' efforts to meet any shortfall in generation this summer included activation of mothballed units; arrangement to import up to 2,500 megawatts (MW) of electricity; and financial incentives for customers to shift from guaranteed to interruptible electric load.
Connecticut Lighting and Power Co (CL&P), a subsidiary of Northeast Utilities, retooled some of its generating units ahead of the winter season.
"We are doing maintenance...They've been winterizing units," said NU spokeswoman Myra Humphrey.
For example, CL&P upgraded four 40 MW turbines that were installed at the Devon station this spring so they could consume either jet fuel or natural gas this winter, she said.
Earlier this month, CL&P and UI submitted to the state's Department of Public Utilities plans to offer deals to selected customers to shift their winter load.
Concerns about Connecticut's winter power supply as well as New England are tempered because peak winter demand is much less than summer loads.

"It's nowhere near a concern at this point...We're not as concerned about it as the summer," said William Shepherdson, spokesman for the New England Power Pool (NEPOOL), which oversees the area's power planning and reliable transmission.
"The pool's exposure is 1,500 MW lower in the winter than in the summer," Shepherdson said.
During a typical winter day, demand tops at midday, ebbs, then surges again when individuals return home from work, switching on residential lights, Mayko said.
In a typical summer day, electric demand peaks from midday through early evening tied to a steady air-conditioning load.
UI's record summer peak was set Aug 23, 1991 at 1,161 MW, against its highest winter peak of 914 MW on Dec 11, 1995.
The four Connecticut nuclear stations provide about three-fourths of the state's electricity output.
The 582 MW Connecticut Yankee nuclear power plant was taken off line July 22 for a repair and refueling outage.

The shutdown is shadowed by new safety worries after a Nuclear Regulatory Commission inspection this summer. On Oct 9, Connecticut Yankee said the plant could be permanently shut after analysis showed it may be too costly to run.
All three Millstone units, with combined capacity near 2,700 MW, have been shut since March 31 amid safety concerns.
Restart of any Millstone units remained uncertain, but industry sources suggested NU, which operates Millstone, would start the 1,150 MW Millstone unit 3 at the end of 1996.

"We are anticipating a small surplus above the (winter) peak load including those outages," Shepherdson said, adding NEPOOL has not surpassed 19,722 MW, the winter peak set in January 1989, so far in the 1990s. The pool projected a fifty percent chance it would hit the 19,600 MW mark this winter.
